items.title: Payroll and pensions
items.source: Draft for review. Written by an AI assistant from general UK small-business knowledge, not from a cited document. Check every fact against current GOV.UK and regulator guidance, and have someone who does this work review it, before it is activated. Rules differ by country and change.
items.body: If you employ someone you must run payroll. Each time you pay, work out gross pay, deduct income tax and employee National Insurance, add employer National Insurance, and report to the tax authority (in the UK, through PAYE, in real time). Pay at least the national minimum or living wage for the worker's age. Give each worker a payslip. Eligible workers must be enrolled automatically into a workplace pension, with the employer paying in too, and you must keep records. Mistakes cost the employee first, so use payroll software or a payroll provider and check with an accountant what applies to you.

options.text: Deducts income tax and National Insurance from pay and sends it to the tax authority
Asks the employee to pay tax once a year

questions.prompt: Under automatic enrolment, who must be put into a workplace pension?

options.text: Anyone who asks, but nobody else
Eligible workers, unless they opt out
Nobody, because pensions are optional for employers

questions.prompt: What is a sensible way to avoid payroll mistakes?

options.text: Guess the deductions and correct them later

Use payroll software or a provider, and have an accountant confirm what applies

items.title: Discipline and dismissal
items.source: Draft for review. Written by an AI assistant from general UK small-business knowledge, not from a cited document. Check every fact against current GOV.UK and regulator guidance, and have someone who does this work review it, before it is activated. Rules differ by country and change.
items.body: Treat a performance or conduct problem as a process, not an outburst. Start by raising it clearly and informally. If it continues, investigate the facts, tell the employee in writing what the concern is, hold a meeting where they can explain and bring a companion, decide and give the outcome in writing, and offer a right to appeal. Warnings usually build in steps and are proportionate to the problem; serious misconduct can justify a faster route but still needs a fair investigation. Dismissal must be for a fair reason, such as conduct, capability or redundancy, and be handled fairly. Keep notes of every step. Take employment advice before any formal step, because rules and qualifying periods change.

items.body: A fair pay system is one people can understand. Set pay bands for each role, based on what the role does and what the market pays, and place people within a band by clear criteria such as skill and experience, not by who negotiates hardest. Employers must give equal pay for equal work or work of equal value regardless of protected characteristics such as sex, and unexplained gaps are a risk. Review pay on a regular cycle, explain the decision, and link progression to published criteria for the next level. Be open about how a rise or promotion is earned; secret, inconsistent pay breeds unfairness and turnover.

options.text: It stops anyone getting a rise

items.body: Hire on evidence, not impression. Write down what the job needs before you advertise: the tasks, the skills that matter and the pay. Use the same questions and the same scoring for every candidate, based on the role, and keep notes; this is fairer and more reliable than a relaxed chat. A short, realistic task shows more than a CV. Check references and the right to work before the start date. Do not ask about protected characteristics such as age, health or plans for children, and avoid choosing people because they remind you of yourself. Tell unsuccessful candidates promptly; it protects your reputation.

options.text: It makes the comparison fairer and more reliable

options.text: Describe a time you solved a problem

items.body: Before someone starts, agree and write down the terms. In the UK a worker or employee is entitled to a written statement of main terms from the first day: who the parties are, job title, start date, pay and how often, hours, holiday, notice, where they work, and any probation. Pay must meet the national minimum or living wage. Decide whether the person is an employee, a worker or genuinely self-employed, because it changes rights, tax and insurance; calling someone self-employed does not make them so. Give people a contract they can understand and keep a signed copy.

items.title: Stress and burnout at work

items.body: Stress is a normal reaction to pressure, but long-lasting pressure with no recovery becomes burnout: exhaustion, cynicism and falling performance. Employers have a duty to look after employees' health, including from work-related stress. Signs include irritability, more mistakes, absence, withdrawal and very long hours. Prevent it by balancing workload with capacity, giving people control over how they work, setting clear expectations, supporting them as a manager, and allowing real rest. When someone shows signs, talk privately, listen, and change the work; do not just tell them to cope. For an individual who is unwell, point them to occupational health or their doctor.

questions.prompt: What is burnout?

options.text: Long-lasting exhaustion from pressure without recovery

questions.prompt: Which is a common sign of work stress?

options.text: Unusually high energy and fewer mistakes
Higher team spirit and fewer absences

questions.prompt: What is the best first step when someone shows signs of burnout?

options.text: Give them more work to keep them busy
Talk privately, listen and look at their workload

questions.prompt: Which change best reduces the risk of stress across a team?

options.text: Balancing workload with capacity and giving people control over their work

items.title: Delegating and one-to-ones
items.source: Draft for review. Written by an AI assistant from general UK small-business knowledge, not from a cited document. Check every fact against current GOV.UK and regulator guidance, and have someone who does this work review it, before it is activated. Rules differ by country and change.
items.body: Delegating means handing over a task and the authority to do it, while you stay accountable for the result. Describe the outcome you want, not every step; give a deadline, the information and the authority needed, agree when you will check in, and then let the person do it their way. Taking a task back at the first stumble teaches people to wait for you. A one-to-one is a regular private meeting, often weekly or fortnightly, where the employee sets much of the agenda: what is in the way, what they need, how they are, and what feedback you can both give. Keep it even when busy; cancelling it tells people they are not a priority.

options.text: A meeting only for disciplinary action
A regular private meeting between a manager and one team member

options.text: Nothing, so they work it out alone

What does cancelling one-to-ones repeatedly tend to signal?

options.text: That they are doing very well
That the person is not a priority
That the manager is delegating well

items.body: Culture is how people actually behave when nobody is watching. Values only matter when they are lived. Choose a few values you really mean, describe them as behaviours people can see, and use them to decide who to hire, reward, promote and part with. Leaders set the culture most by what they do, so their conduct must match what they say. Notice what you tolerate: what is allowed becomes the norm. Ask staff how it feels to work there and listen. Culture changes slowly through consistent small actions, not posters or one-off events.

items.body: Growing the team well means hiring for the work ahead and changing how you organise as numbers grow. Before adding people, check what the work needs, whether a process change would fix the pressure, and whether you can afford the person for a year. Decide the role and who they report to. As the team grows, the founder cannot manage everyone: define roles, give managers authority and make decisions at the right level. Keep communication regular so people know the plan. Watch for the stage when informal habits stop working and write down what matters, such as how decisions are made.

items.body: How you tell staff about important news shows what you think of them. Tell people early, in person where you can, and before they hear it elsewhere. Be clear about what is happening, why, what it means for them and what happens next, including what you do not yet know. Allow questions and listen. Follow with something in writing. Where jobs are affected, legal rules on consultation, notice and fair selection apply, so take advice before you announce anything. Treat people with respect and honesty, and support those who leave. How you handle bad news is remembered for years.
